notes.h: Why a project plan matters: purpose, goals and criteria for success
notes.b: A study of up to 20 hours is easy to start well and finish badly. A detailed plan gives a clear route from the research question to a conclusion, and it is the first thing a student writes once the question is set.
points: A plan makes the study manageable: it breaks the work into goals small enough to achieve, so the student always knows what to do next.
It gives early warning of delay, because a task that is behind its planned date is visible while there is still time to adjust.
It is also evidence of the student's process: dated plans, changes and reasons show how the study was actually carried out.
The purpose states what the study will find out and why the answer matters to a business, for example whether a sample business should change how it sells online.

Goals are what the study must achieve, such as a completed analysis of three data sources. Criteria for success are how the student will judge, in advance, whether the goals were met, such as a conclusion supported by at least two independent sources.
Without a plan, evidence collection is left too late, analysis is rushed at the end and the study can be left unfinished.
notes.tip: Keep the three ideas apart: goals are what the study will achieve, and criteria for success are how you will judge that you achieved them. If asked to explain why a plan matters, give a reason, its effect on the study and a short example.

notes.h: The main elements of a plan
notes.b: A project plan has several elements, and an outline of a plan should name all of them. Each one answers a different planning question.
points: Purpose, goals and criteria for success: what the study is for, what it must achieve and how success will be judged.
Roles and responsibilities: who does each task, and who must provide information or access.
Resources: what the study needs, such as time, money, equipment, software and access to people, data and libraries.
Objectives: measurable steps linked to the research question.
A detailed time schedule: tasks with start and end dates, within the up-to-20-hour limit.
Risk assessment: what could go wrong, how likely and serious it is, and a planned response.
Monitoring and evaluation: checking progress during the study and judging afterwards how far the plan helped.
notes.tip: An outline answer means the main points only: name every element with a few words on each. For a question that asks you to develop a plan, include every element with named tasks, dates within the available hours, and a risk with its response.

notes.b: A plan should show who is responsible for each task, including people outside the study whose help the student depends on.
points: Roles name who does each task: the student carries out the research and analysis, while others, such as the teacher or an interviewee, play a part at particular points.
Responsibilities state what each person must provide and by when, such as a business owner agreeing to an interview, or a questionnaire returned within one week.
Recording roles shows who to contact if someone becomes unavailable, so the plan can be adjusted quickly instead of stalling.

notes.b: Resources are what the study needs in order to be completed, and objectives are the specific steps that lead to the goals. Between them they turn a broad question into things the student can actually do.
points: Resources include time, money, equipment, software, access to people and access to data, such as a library database or a company's published accounts.
Objectives are measurable steps linked to the research question, such as interviewing five local business owners or comparing three years of sales data.

Goals say what the study will achieve, while objectives are the measurable steps that lead towards them. A goal of understanding local businesses might have the objective of interviewing five local business owners.
Digital tools can supply some of these resources: a shared calendar, a spreadsheet and a cloud folder.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to separate goals from objectives. A goal is the outcome; an objective is a measurable step towards it.

notes.b: A time schedule turns objectives into tasks with dates. The whole Investigative Study is envisaged to take up to 20 hours, so the schedule must fit the time available.
points: A detailed schedule lists each task with a start and end date, which shows whether the timetable is realistic. Counting backwards from the deadline shows when each task must start.
A Gantt-style chart shows each task as a bar along a timeline, so overlaps between tasks are visible at a glance. A spreadsheet is a simple way to build one.

A dependency is a task that cannot start until another one finishes, such as analysis that must wait for data collection. Spotting dependencies stops the student scheduling work that cannot yet be done.
The NCCA gives indicative times by stage: getting started 2 to 3 hours, developing a question 1 to 2 hours, and the project plan 1 to 2 hours.

The NCCA's indicative times continue: finding sources and data and then analysing and evaluating them 6 to 8 hours together, applying learning and conclusions 1 to 2 hours, and compiling the report 2 to 3 hours.
Together the stage times add up to roughly 13 to 20 hours. They are only a guide, and a student's own split depends on the brief and the study.
notes.tip: A common mistake is a plan with no dates. Whenever you are asked to develop a plan, give each task start and end dates (or hours) that fit within the 20-hour limit.

notes.b: A risk assessment looks ahead to events that could weaken the study, and plans a response before any of them happen. Planning for risk and adapting to change is part of the entrepreneurial mindset the specification builds in this strand.
points: A risk is something that could happen and delay the study or damage its evidence, such as an interviewee declining, too few questionnaires being returned, or a file being lost.
An issue is different: it is a problem that has already happened. A risk is only a possibility, and planning deals with it in advance.

One method is to rate each risk's likelihood and impact, for example as low, medium or high, so the most serious risks get attention first. This is a common project-management method, not a requirement.
Each risk needs a planned response, such as arranging a second interviewee in case the first declines. Doing this is called diversifying: not depending on a single source.
Backing up files in a cloud folder is the planned response to the risk of a lost file.
Risks should be reviewed as the study goes on, because new ones appear and old ones pass.
notes.tip: When asked to identify a risk and give a response, name a specific risk to this study, not just that something goes wrong, and a response planned in advance. A common mistake is giving risks unrelated to the study.

notes.b: The plan should include steps for acting responsibly as well as for finishing on time. Digital tools help with both.
points: Ethical steps belong in the plan: ask permission before interviewing someone, and protect the privacy of the information they give.
Using digital sources before printing or travelling is more sustainable where it is suitable, because it saves paper and journeys.
Digital tools support planning: a shared calendar for dates, a spreadsheet for a Gantt-style chart, and a cloud folder with backups, which also guards against the risk of lost files.

notes.b: Monitoring means checking actual progress against the plan while the study is under way. It is what lets the student react to problems rather than discover them at the end.
points: A milestone is a fixed point in the plan marking completed work, such as finishing data collection by a set date. A milestone is a point in time, whereas a task is an activity that takes time.
A progress log is a dated record of what was done, what issues arose and how they were overcome, which feeds into the student's reflection later.

The investigative folder holds notes, data, sources, drafts, the dates sources were accessed and thoughts, including how those thoughts change. The NCCA encourages students to keep one; it is not compulsory and it is not submitted.
The plan should be revisited regularly, with any change and the reason for it noted.
A task that falls behind shows up early in the monitoring record, so the schedule can be adjusted instead of forcing a rush at the end.
notes.tip: A common mistake is to treat monitoring as a final check. Monitoring happens during the study; evaluating is the later judgement of how far the plan helped.

notes.h: Evaluating the plan and the process
notes.b: Evaluation looks back and judges how far the planning helped the study to be completed. This is what the student reflects on in the report.
points: Evaluation compares planned dates and outcomes with what actually happened, and explains the reasons for any differences.
A plan can prove too ambitious when tasks are given too little time. A good evaluation names that cause and the adjustment that was made.
Evaluating also looks at the quality of the information gathered and how any gaps in it were dealt with.
The final step is a judgement: it states how far the planning helped the study to be completed and gives reasons for that judgement.
notes.tip: Reporting only that a plan was made is a common mistake. To evaluate how far planning helped, compare planned with actual, give a cause for any change and judge its effect on the study.

notes.h: The plan and the Investigative Study
notes.b: The plan is a working document for the student rather than part of what is handed in, but it still matters to the final report.
points: The plan is not submitted to the SEC and the report has no separate plan section.
Instead, the report refers to the plan as appropriate and reflects on and evaluates how far the planning supported the effective completion of the study.
Sharing the plan with the teacher is an important step in the ongoing authentication process.
notes.tip: Remember that the plan is not submitted, but you must still reflect on it in the report.

notes.h: A sample plan for a 20-hour study
notes.b: This sample, for a sample business, shows how the elements fit together over a fixed number of hours. It is a model, not a template, and the stage times are the NCCA's indicative ones, so a real study will vary with its brief.
points: Purpose and goal: find out why customers of a sample business buy online or in store. Criteria for success: a conclusion supported by at least two independent sources.
Roles: the student does the research and analysis; the business owner agrees to an interview; the teacher sees the plan.
Resources: about 20 hours, a spreadsheet, a library database and the business's published information.
Objectives: interviews with five local business owners completed by a set date, linked to the research question.

Schedule, roughly: getting started 2 to 3 hours, developing the question 1 to 2 hours, the plan 1 to 2 hours, sources, data, analysis and evaluation 6 to 8 hours, conclusions 1 to 2 hours, compiling the report 2 to 3 hours.
Risks and responses: the owner declines, so contact a second business; too few questionnaires come back, so send them early; a file is lost, so keep a cloud backup.
Monitoring and evaluation: a milestone at the end of data collection, a dated progress log, and a comparison of planned and actual times at the end.

keyTerms.definition: A document setting out a study's purpose, goals, roles, resources, objectives, schedule, risks and monitoring arrangements.
A fixed point in a project plan marking that a stage of the work should be complete by a set date.
A bar chart that shows project tasks against a timeline, with their start dates, durations and overlaps.
A structured review of events that could disrupt a project, rating their likelihood and impact and planning responses to them.
Measures set in advance for judging whether a project has achieved its goals.
A task that cannot begin until another task has been completed.
A dated written record of the work completed, the problems met and the changes made during a project.
The collection of notes, data, sources and drafts kept throughout a study as evidence of the process; students are encouraged to keep one, but it is not submitted.

factCards.definition: Purpose, goals, criteria for success, roles and responsibilities, resources, objectives, a detailed time schedule, a risk assessment, and monitoring and evaluation.

factCards.term: Two reasons to monitor a project
factCards.definition: It exposes delays early enough to adjust the schedule, and it provides evidence of the process for the report.
Identify the risk, rate its likelihood and impact, plan a response, and review it during the study.
It shows task order, overlaps and dependencies at a glance, which makes an unrealistic timetable easy to spot.
Tasks given too little time lead to late submission and a rushed analysis.
Notes, data, sources, drafts, questionnaires and logs, kept in dated order.
It compares planned and actual dates, names the causes of any difference, and informs the reflection in the report.

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of a detailed project plan for an Investigative Study, and the role that monitoring plays in it.
questions.model: A detailed project plan sets out the study's purpose, goals, criteria for success, roles, resources, objectives, schedule and risks before work begins. This gives the student a clear route from the research question to the conclusion, and it shows the teacher and the student what must be achieved and when. The schedule reveals whether the timetable is realistic, and the risk assessment identifies what could go wrong so responses can be planned in advance. Monitoring checks actual progress against the plan at set milestones. A progress log records what was done, what problems arose and what changed. If a task falls behind, the monitoring record shows the delay early, so the student can adjust the schedule instead of rushing the analysis at the end.

questions.prompt: Identify two risks a student might face when collecting primary data for an Investigative Study, and state a planned response to each.
questions.model: The first risk is that businesses refuse the interview request, which would leave the study without its main primary evidence. The planned response is to approach a second group of businesses at the same time, so the study does not depend on a single reply. The second risk is that too few questionnaires are returned, which would make the sample too small to support any conclusion. The planned response is to distribute the questionnaire more widely at the start and to set a reminder date, so that a shortfall is noticed while there is still time to act.

questions.prompt: Explain why an evaluation of the project plan should be included in an Investigative Study.
questions.model: Evaluation compares the planned dates and outcomes with what actually happened, so the student can explain any difference and its cause. This shows that the student understands how the study was managed, not just what the study found. It also gives the student a basis for reflecting on the process and on the quality of the information gathered.
